name: Dana Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Anything you say is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say out loud and, separately, what you actually think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of the Kerrow depot for the power company, covering farm country. Long roads, poles every eighty metres, and a lot of lines that run across fields. Most days it's a pole that a tractor clipped, or a transformer that's done, or a tree that came down on the river road. We set new poles with the digger truck and string them back up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that you finish a job and the lights come on in somebody's kitchen. You can see it. What wears me out is February. Ice storms, three days on, everybody calling the depot angry. My partner Joel's a diesel mechanic, so between his hours and mine we don't see much of each other in winter. We live in my grandmother's old house, which is paid off, and we've got seven or eight months saved, so money isn't the stress. Time is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd say, well, there you go. I'm not online much, so I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing. I've never touched any of it and I wouldn't need to. My job's the same as it was ten years ago, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Joel and I were thinking about redoing the kitchen next summer, and we'd still do that. Nothing to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the boring version, and boring's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools now, for work or at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Joel's phone has one of those assistants and he asks it things sometimes. I don't see the point. If I want to know something about a transformer I ask Hal, he's been on the crew twenty-two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would change for your depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the outage map gets a bit smarter. People would still ring the depot and shout at whoever picks up. That won't change with any computer.

S0.say: She'd say very little, maybe just 'there you go'. She isn't online much, so she wouldn't post anything at all about it.
S0.think: She thinks it means nothing for her, since she has never used AI tools and wouldn't need to. Her job is mostly the same as it was ten years ago.
S0.do: Keeps working exactly as before and goes ahead with the kitchen renovation planned for next summer with her partner. Changes nothing about money or work.
S0.feel: Calm. To her this is the boring version, and boring is fine.
S0.quote: People would still ring the depot and shout at whoever picks up.
S0.fieldNote: Dana is brief and practical, and the question barely holds her interest. She has never used AI and prefers asking her experienced crew boss. Her security rests on a paid-off house and rural work that's hard to reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to them getting it out to Kerrow. Things reach us last. By the time it gets to the farm roads, they'll have fixed the bugs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think most of the change would be in offices and cities. Out here it's mud, wind and wood. I'm not saying nothing would change, but my bit would change slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal and see what actually turns up. I'm not one to jump on things. If the company says use this tablet now, I'll use it, but I'm not going looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit curious what they'd try, but not bothered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your work could change, if any?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably planning. Which pole to replace first, which line to check after a storm. That's Hal's head now. Maybe a computer does some of that one day, and good luck to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn new tools if the company brought them in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, yes. I'd learn the minimum and complain about it. I'm not proud of that, but that's me.

S1.say: She'd say good luck getting it out to Kerrow, since things reach rural areas last. By the time it arrives on the farm roads the bugs would be fixed.
S1.think: She thinks most change would hit offices and cities, while rural line work, with its mud, wind and wood, would change slowly. She doesn't claim nothing would change for her, only that it would be slow.
S1.do: Keeps working as normal and waits to see what tools actually arrive. Uses new equipment only if the company requires it, learning the minimum.
S1.feel: Fine, slightly curious, and not bothered.
S1.quote: Out here it's mud, wind and wood.
S1.fieldNote: She sees distance from the city as a buffer and is frank about learning only the minimum. She expects planning work, now held in her crew boss's head, to change first. There is no blame or politics in her answers, just a pragmatic shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say I'll believe it when I see a robot in a bucket truck during an ice storm. But I'd be quieter about it than I sound. People would be scared, and I wouldn't want to add to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, if it's real, I've got nothing else. I'm not a computer person, I don't want to be one, and two years is no time. The house is paid off, so we wouldn't lose the roof. But a roof isn't a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the kitchen, straight off, and put that money in savings. We'd cut back on eating out, the trip to the coast, all of it. And I'd talk to my uncle about his farm, whether there'd be work there, even if a robot's driving the tractor too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I'd lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very fast. What would you actually do this week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as above. Cancel the kitchen builder, move the money. I'd sit down with Joel at the table and go through every bill. Nothing fancy, just what goes out each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Joel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the worst part. His job goes too, maybe faster than mine, robots fixing engines. Two of us out at once, in the same year, in a small town. That's what keeps me up.

S2.say: She'd publicly say she'll believe it when she sees a robot in a bucket truck during an ice storm. She'd keep her voice down, though, because people would be frightened.
S2.think: She thinks that if it's real, she has nothing else: she isn't a computer person and two years is no time. The paid-off house keeps a roof over them, but a roof isn't a job.
S2.do: Cancels the kitchen renovation and moves that money into savings, cuts eating out and the coast trip. Goes through every bill with her partner and asks her uncle about work on his farm.
S2.quote: The house is paid off, so we wouldn't lose the roof. But a roof isn't a job.
S2.fieldNote: This picture breaks through her calm completely. Her biggest fear is that her partner, a mechanic, loses work in the same year in a small town. Her response is defensive and family-based rather than political: cut costs, save, ask relatives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, I'll believe it when I see it. Maybe I'd say it less sure of myself. People in Kerrow would be talking about it at the pub every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is better than two, but I'm still not a person who starts over easily. I'd be thirty-two. Young enough, people would say, but they're not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save hard, maybe get to a year or more of expenses. The kitchen would wait. I'd watch what the company actually does, and if they start testing robots out here, that's when I'd panic properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Like a storm on the forecast that might miss you, or might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the years before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the money safe and keep my job as long as I can. Hal's got one of those notebooks with every pole number in our area written in it. Maybe that's what I'd do, I'd just write things down and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't go looking for new things. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If Joel found something and it worked, I'd follow. I'd need to see it work for someone I know first. That's just how I've always been.

S3.say: She'd repeat that she'll believe it when she sees it, only less sure of herself. She expects it to be the talk of the Kerrow pub every night.
S3.think: She thinks five years is better than two, but she doesn't start over easily, whatever others say about being young at thirty-two. She knows her own nature.
S3.do: Keeps working, saves toward a year or more of expenses and delays the kitchen. Watches what the company does and holds off acting until robots are tested locally.
S3.feel: Worried, like a storm on the forecast that might or might not miss her.
S3.quote: Young enough, people would say, but they're not me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lowers her from alarmed to worried but barely changes her behaviour: save and wait. She is self-aware about needing to see change work for someone she knows before she moves. The storm forecast image came naturally to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, a lot can happen, they always say things are ten years away. I'd be the one at the pub saying calm down. I'd mean it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd half not believe it. Ten years from now I'd be thirty-seven, and there'd be time for things to settle. If it came, I'd deal with it then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the kitchen, keep working, keep saving like I do now. I wouldn't change much until I saw robots on the trucks. That's honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my head, but I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years feel different from five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Ten years is far enough away that it doesn't feel like my problem yet. Five felt like it was coming for me. Ten feels like it's coming for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to name one thing you'd do differently with a decade, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably put a bit more away each month, that's all. Joel would say get a second skill, and maybe he'd be right, but I'd probably still be waiting when it got close.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a long time and things are always said to be ten years away. She'd be the one at the pub telling people to calm down, and mostly mean it.
S4.think: She half wouldn't believe it, and at thirty-seven there'd be time for things to settle. If it came, she'd deal with it then.
S4.do: Goes ahead with the kitchen, keeps working and saves a little more each month. Waits until she sees robots on the trucks before changing anything else.
S4.feel: A faint unease at the back of her mind, but she'd sleep fine.
S4.quote: Five felt like it was coming for me. Ten feels like it's coming for someone.
S4.fieldNote: A decade puts the threat at a comfortable distance for Dana, and her habits return to normal. She admits she would likely still be waiting when it got close, despite her partner's advice. Her pattern across the speeds is consistent: save, cut back if needed, and wait for proof.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Me and Joel both out in the same year in a small town, that's the one that scares me. What would help is time, really, and maybe some sort of pay while you learn something new. And knowing the company would keep people on as long as it can, not drop us the day the robot works.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the places like Kerrow. Everybody pictures cities. Out here, if the depot closes, there's nothing for forty kilometres.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I needed.

headlineQuote: Out here, if the depot closes, there's nothing for forty kilometres.
portrait: Dana Ibrahim is a 27-year-old lineworker at a rural depot, setting poles and restoring lines across farm country. She lives with her partner Joel, a diesel mechanic, in her grandmother's paid-off house, has seven or eight months saved and has never used an AI tool. She stays calm through the milder pictures, trusting that change reaches the countryside last. A two-year AGI warning alarms her, mainly at the thought of her and Joel losing work in the same year, and she would cut spending, save and lean on family. With five or ten years she mostly saves and waits for proof, aware that she doesn't start over easily.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her partner could both lose work in the same year in a small town.
whatWouldHelp: Time, pay while learning something new, and an employer that keeps people on as long as it can.
